content.title: About
content.content: Escarole (Cichorium endivia) is a leafy vegetable from the Asteraceae family. Cooked escarole has a tender texture and a mild, slightly bitter flavor. It is commonly used in soups, stews, casseroles, and as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Escarole belongs to the same genus as chicory and endive.
Heat softens its bitterness and brings out a nutty aroma.
It is grown in temperate regions; major producers include the United States, Italy, and France.
The leaves are rich in chlorophyll, giving them a vivid green color.
In cooking, escarole is often substituted for spinach or kale.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K supports blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains vitamin A and folate
items.content: Important for vision, immune function, and cell growth.

items.title: Good source of dietary fiber
items.content: Helps regulate digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Ideal for weight‑management diets because it provides volume with few calories.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Asteraceae allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to vegetables from the Asteraceae family.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Escarole contains oxalates, which in high amounts can contribute to kidney stone formation.

items.title: Nutrient loss with overcooking
items.content: Prolonged heat can reduce the levels of heat‑sensitive vitamins.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked escarole can be added to soups, stews, casseroles, or used as a filling for pies. It is also served as a side dish, lightly sautéed with garlic and olive oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh escarole in the refrigerator in a bag or container with a damp paper towel for 3–5 days. Cooked escarole should be kept in an airtight container in the fridge and consumed within 2–3 days.
